analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting and commercial logging on millions of acres of federal forest land.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban clearcutting and logging in ancient and roadless federal forests drew 122 cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have outlawed clearcutting and other even-age logging on National Forests, BLM land, and wildlife refuges, and banned logging and road building in old-growth forests, roadless areas, watershed protection areas, and dozens of named special areas across 26 states. It would have let ordinary citizens sue to enforce the ban, with mandatory damages of at least $5,000 against violators, including the federal government itself. It was introduced in July 2002, sent to two committees and four subcommittees, and died there without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses federal forests — hikers, hunters, anglers, campers, and the communities that depend on clean water from forested watersheds — plus fish and wildlife habitat and the fishing, hunting, and tourism businesses that depend on it. The bill also argued that the more selective logging it allows is more labor-intensive, supporting more jobs per board-foot of timber.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forest users, anglers, hunters, tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits clearcutting and even-age logging on National Forest System land, BLM land, and National Wildlife Refuge System land, and requires a shift to selective logging or restoration on previously clearcut stands [S2][S3].

Bars road construction and all extractive logging in ancient forests, roadless areas, watershed protection areas, and designated special areas, protecting the drinking water, fisheries, and recreation the bill says these lands provide [S2][S3].

Gives any citizen the right to sue violators — including the United States — for injunctions and statutory damages of at least $5,000, with attorney's fees, and waives the government's sovereign immunity so federal agencies can be taken to court [S3].

The bill's own findings state that extractive logging on federal land runs at 'enormous financial costs to the Treasury and taxpayers,' meaning ending it would have stopped subsidies taxpayers currently fund [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry loses access to federal forest land — the old-growth, roadless, and special areas become off-limits, and the large even-age cuts it relies on are banned everywhere on federal land. Timber-dependent rural towns could see federal timber sales decline, though the bill contends selective logging is more job-intensive per unit of timber.

drawbacks.text: A nationwide ban on even-age logging and permanent statutory protection for named areas would remove flexibility — foresters and some scientists argue that even-age methods, including patches of clearcutting, are legitimate tools for some forest types and can matter for fire management and early-succession wildlife habitat [S3].

The citizen-suit provision requires courts to award at least $5,000 in damages and attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs against any violator, including federal agencies, with no notice requirement — a design that could channel significant resources into litigation rather than forest management [S3].
Reducing the federal timber supply would concentrate more logging on private and state land and could raise costs for sawmills and mill workers in regions that depend on federal timber sales [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the loss of federal timber for permanent protection of old-growth forests, roadless areas, and watersheds, plus an unusually strong citizen-enforcement mechanism. The main honest objections are its rigidity — a blanket ban on even-age forestry written into statute regardless of local forest conditions — and a litigation-friendly enforcement design. For ordinary people the direct cost is small (federal timber is a small share of national wood supply, and the bill says taxpayers lose money on it), while the protected lands are public assets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced late in the session and referred to the Agriculture and Resources Committees, which in turn passed it to four subcommittees in August 2002; neither committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Act to Save America's Forests in the House on July 26, 2002, with 121 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to both the Agriculture Committee and the Resources Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

On August 13, 2002, it was sent to four subcommittees — National Parks, Recreation and Public Lands; Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans; Forests and Forest Health; and Department Operations, Oversight, Nutrition and Forestry — and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
By the end of the session the bill had 122 cosponsors: 119 of 208 House Democrats, 2 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's lone Independent [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place; the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry kept access to federal forests — clearcutting and old-growth logging on public land continued under the same rules as before, and the subsidized federal logging program the bill's findings criticized kept running.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies and the federal logging status quo

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 119 of 208 House Democrats versus 2 of 223 House Republicans — and the bill died in committees chaired by the Republican majority without a vote.

industries.note: The bill bans clearcutting on all federal land and all extractive logging in ancient forests, roadless areas, watersheds, and special areas, cutting off the public-land timber that companies harvest below cost to taxpayers, per the bill's findings. Its gain in continuing access comes at the expense of the public lands and water the bill would protect.

industries.industry: Recreation, fishing, hunting, and tourism businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings say destroying large unfragmented forests has cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding; protecting those forests preserves the product these businesses sell. Their interest runs with the public's.

Shrinking the federal timber supply hits towns and workers built around it, though the bill argues selective logging is more labor-intensive per board-foot than clearcutting. The effect on these communities depends on how quickly mills can adapt.
